guidance.opening:
It is autumn of 1920 in Boston. You sit in a landlord’s small office after answering his notice: he needs someone who can look into a house that will not stay let. Papers and a desk lamp are the only fuss in the room.

Howard Crane leans on the desk. “Last family in there was the Costas. They didn’t finish the lease—they went to an asylum. Neighbors won’t even look at the place now, and I can’t rent it. I want a pair of eyes on what happened, someone who can tell me if the house can be lived in again.”

He taps a pencil once, then looks you over. “So—who are you, and what do you do for a living? Rough answer’s fine.”
guidance.advice: Occupations from the module list only. Strong public fits for a 1920 Boston landlord asking a stranger to look into a house that will not re-let: Private Investigator, Journalist, Police Detective, Police Officer, Lawyer, Librarian, Professor, Author, Antiquarian, Doctor of Medicine, Parapsychologist, Clergy. Others on the list remain valid if the player wants them. Useful training and languages are era-appropriate Boston work: Library Use, History, Law, Occult as rumor-not-fact, Fast Talk, Spot Hidden, Credit Rating; English is assumed, Italian or Latin can be optional flavor only. Belongings: notebook, city clothes, streetcar fare, modest tools—no keys, cash advance, or house address from this meeting. Public involvement: they answered a notice or were sent for; Crane has not hired them yet. Optional ties (not facts): knew a former tenant socially, write for a paper, once treated a nervous patient. Do not invent numbers or force a profession. Authored public facts: Crane is the landlord; last tenants, the Costas, left for an asylum; he wants the property lettable. Do not mention Crowe, chapel, sanitarium names, magic lessons, or keys.
guidance.handoff: The visitor is in Howard Crane’s Boston office in autumn 1920 after answering his notice about a house that will not stay rented. Crane has spoken only of the last tenants (the Costas) leaving for an asylum and of wanting someone to look into whether the place can be lived in again. He has asked who the visitor is and what they do for a living. No hire, fee, keys, address, or items have been given. Continue from that identity question into character setup, then return to the same office conversation.
